claim: The surface structure creates a Marangoni effect where surface tension gradients drive directional transport
mechanism: Temperature or composition differences across the surface create surface tension gradients (Marangoni effect), causing droplets to move from regions of higher surface tension to lower surface tension
evidence: Marangoni effects drive droplet movement on some surfaces
Temperature gradients can influence droplet behavior
Surface tension differences can create directional forces
assumptions: Surface tension gradients can be maintained across the microstructure
Marangoni forces are stronger than other forces acting on droplets
Temperature/composition differences are achievable under field conditions
expected_failure_modes: Insufficient temperature/composition gradient to generate meaningful Marangoni forces
Rapid equalization of gradients preventing sustained transport
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis proposes that surface tension gradients rather than wettability gradients are the primary driving force
testability: Can be tested by measuring temperature/composition gradients across the surface and correlating with transport direction
falsifier: If transport direction reverses when temperature/composition gradient is reversed, or if no transport occurs when temperature/composition gradients are eliminated
